pi-mcp-adapter: # Pi MCP Adapter Use MCP servers with Pi without burning your context window. ## What's new in 7.0 On servers that support MCP Tasks, add `"protocolVersion": "auto"` and slow tools run in the background while the agent keeps working. Tool search can rank tools by meaning and send full schemas only for the ones that fit. And `extract` hands the agent just the values it asked for from a long result. Everything else is in the changelog. ## Why This Exists Mario wrote about why you might not need MCP. The problem: tool definitions are verbose. A single MCP server can burn 10k+ tokens, and you're paying that cost whether you use those tools or not. Connect a few servers and you've burned half your context window before the conversation starts. His take: skip MCP entirely, write simple CLI tools

They have to be loaded into context, correctly interpreted, and remembered turns later, and none of that is guaranteed on any given run. Prose decays: it drifts out of context, gets skimmed instead of read, or is outweighed by whatever the agent is focused on in the moment. A lint rule has none of these failure modes: it runs on every diff, every time, and fails the build instead of hoping to be noticed. Every rule and every shared config in this package

pi-session-surgery: # pi-session-surgery A Pi extension that keeps long-running sessions small on disk. Everything before that boundary is never sent to the model. The moment Pi reports a successful compaction, the extension rewrites the session file in place and drops the invisible messages, plus the older compaction records. The part the model can see is copied unchanged, so what the model receives does not change. pi-worktree-guard: # pi-worktree-guard **Agents writing into a repository's primary checkout is not a hypothetical. On one repository I measured it directly: twenty-nine sessions, twenty-four of them overlapping in time, all editing the same checkout at once. What they left behind was twelve orphaned index entries that nobody could attribute to anything.** The usual answer is a convention: agents should work in worktrees. Conventions have a hole you can drive through. A session launched in the primary checkout writes straight into it, because nothing is watching. Pi's core is aware of worktrees but never enforces them; the subagent systems isolate their children and leave top-level sessions free to roam; pi has no way to set a session's working directory. The convention exists. The gate does not. pi-worktree

@igor-guari/pi-watch: # pi-watch Wait for anything **without blocking the turn** in the Pi coding agent. The agent registers a **goal**, a **success** condition, an optional **failure** condition and a **deadline**. It ends its turn right away — you get Pi back — and when the condition is met (or the deadline expires) the extension **wakes Pi up** with the goal and the observed data so it can continue. No `sleep`. No `for … sleep 15; done` loops. No bash timeouts. pi-watch demo ## Why Without it, waiting looks like this — the turn is stuck on *Working* for minutes, the loop races the bash timeout, and you can't use Pi meanwhile: before: polling the npm registry inside bash With pi-watch the same wait is one tool call; the turn ends in seconds and Pi resumes on its own when the registry shows the new version. ##

@zeroclover/pi-retry: # pi-retry Automatic retry for failed model requests in Pi. Pi's built-in retry decides by wording alone: after its overflow check, it checks a deny list before an allow list. Its waits are capped by `retry.maxAgentDelayMs` (60 s by default), and only its provider-level retry honours `retry-after`. As a result, a 429 asking to wait 90 s fails after three quick retries, and unrecognised transient errors are never retried. pi-retry steps in once Pi gives up, classifying the error and waiting as long as the provider asks. - Classifies errors by category and stops immediately on deterministic failures (auth, invalid request, context overflow, …). - Honours provider-requested waits from headers, diagnostics, or error text up to a configurable limit, and backs off exponentially with jitter other

@mikefreno/pi-fold: # pi-fold Fold-once context compaction for pi. Each span of a session is summarised exactly once, and every folded span stays restorable in full. ## Why Pi's compaction summarises the span since the previous kept boundary **together with the previous summary**: ``` compaction 1: summary(span 1) compaction 2: summary(summary(span 1) + span 2) compaction 3: summary(summary(summary(span 1) + span 2) + span 3) ``` So the oldest content in a long session is re-abstracted once per compaction, and detail decays geometrically. One opaque blob also means you cannot ask "what did the user say about the auth flow 300 turns back" and get anything back. This extension injects the measured figure before every turn, and challenges the model when it quotes something else. ## What it fixes Three failures, in order of how much they cost: **Fabricated figures.** A model that says "few percent left" is guessing, and the guess is often confidently wrong in both directions: it declares itself nearly out of context and compacts early, or claims plenty of headroom and gets truncated mid-task. **Stale running totals.** A model tracking usage turn-by-turn accumulates a number that only goes up.

@vieko/pi-redact: # pi-redact A pi extension that keeps secrets out of session transcripts. A key that you paste, that a tool prints, or that sits in `AGENTS.md` becomes a stable placeholder such as `[REDACTED-SECRET-5c1e9a7b]`. The model works with the placeholder. pi-reply-reader: # pi-reply-reader Read a Pi or Gentle Shell reply aloud, only when you ask. `/read` takes the latest reply (or one by ID), cleans its Markdown so it sounds like prose instead of "asterisco asterisco", and speaks it with a local Spanish voice. The output can be this machine's speakers or another machine you reach over SSH. `/read notes.md` reads a Markdown file the same way. - **Nothing plays by itself.** A reading starts only with `/read`. @pify/workflow: # @pify/workflow CI npm version npm downloads Deterministic multi-step agent orchestration for pi. The model writes a small JavaScript script that fans work out across child agents, cross-checks the results, and returns one synthesised answer. Intermediate work stays in script variables rather than your chat context. Part of the Pify suite. Install with `pify install workflow` or `pi install npm:@pify/workflow`. ## Why Fan-out is easy; *structured* fan-out is not. As soon as one step's output feeds the next, or findings need verifying by someone who did not produce them, the orchestration itself becomes the interesting part — and asking a model to hold that shape in its head across twenty tool calls is how steps get skipped. @stagefright5/pi-side-agent: # Side Agent Open an independent, fully capable side agent beside the main Pi conversation, in a right-hand Rex split of the same tab. Back to the extension workspace The side agent starts as a copy of the main conversation through its last completed turn. It then continues on its own, as a separate Pi process with its own session file, the same working directory, and the same configured extensions, skills, MCP servers, and tools. Nothing from the side agent reaches the main conversation unless you send a result back and accept it. This is one Rex session with two independent Pi sessions. The two processes never write the same transcript. ## Commands | Command | Where | Behavior | | -------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
